terms.comment: Latin has no word for a dozen and does not count in dozens: a dozen eggs are duodecim ōva.

terms.gloss: twelve each, twelve at a time
evidence: Cic. Agr. 2.85: duodēna dēscrībit in singulōs hominēs jūgera (Lewis & Short)
Caes. B.G. 7.36.7: fossa duplex duodēnum pedum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Twelve to each person or thing; also twelve with nouns used only in the plural (see pair, on bīnī).

evidence: Cic. Att. 7.2.3: quās ego sescentās ūnō tempore accēpī
Ter. Ph. 668: sexcentās proinde scrībitō jam mihi dicās
terms.comment: Properly six hundred; where English says “dozens” or “hundreds”, Latin says six hundred, very often in prose and verse (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: veniō ad epistulās tuās; quās ego sescentās ūnō tempore accēpī, aliam aliā jūcundiōrem
phrases.english: I come to your letters: I got dozens of them at once, each more delightful than the last
Buy a dozen eggs, will you?

sources: Lewis & Short: duodecim · Lewis & Short: duodeni · Lewis & Short: sescenti
Cicero (Att. 7.2.3) and Terence (Ph. 668, in the edition’s spelling sexcentās) checked against the Perseus Latin texts (11 November 2026).
Citations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j).
The example sentences marked “composed” are ours.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency.
